verdict.justification: Deliverable A demonstrates vastly superior strategic and operational acumen by unlocking the hidden value in the prompt's constraints. Because LPI can ramp up to 2,500 units/month (or even at their base 1,500/month) while LiIon only needs 800/month, Deliverable A realizes that LiIon does not need LPI to stay for 6 months—it only needs LPI to do a Last-Time Build (LTB) of ~5,200 sets over ~7 additional weeks and do an early "plastics mould-out" in Weeks 1–3 so the plastic tooling can be released by Week 4. This solves both the supplier's desire for a fast exit and the critical path problem of transferring existing tooling vs. re-developing plastics. Deliverable B misses this operational synergy completely, asking an inflexible, hostile supplier for a 6-to-7-month ongoing transition and proposing that if tooling isn't released by Day 45, LiIon should just "commit to new tools locally" rather than utilizing the paid-for tools early. Furthermore, Deliverable A presents a structured, multi-variable ZOPA table and a punchy executive meeting roadmap that reads like a genuine automotive purchasing playbook.

decisive_issues.issue: Fails to leverage LPI's 2,500/month ramp capacity to compress the exit timeline via a quick Last-Time Build, instead asking a hostile supplier to stay on for up to 7 months.
